content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a method named RNNS to generate adversarial code examples for pre-trained code models. The method replaces a variable name with similar ones nearby until the model makes mistakes. Experiments show that RNNS outperforms the state-of-the-art black-box attacking method (MHM) in terms of both attack success rate and the quality of generated adversarial examples.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

. A nearest neighbor search-based method for searching the adversarial examples.

Weaknesses:

. Only considers variable name substitution

. Lack of comparison with related work.

. More technical details are needed.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is generally well written. The prototypical implementation of the method is available.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The proposed method considers only the variable name substitution. As the authors mentioned, there are other ways to keep the semantics unchanged such as modifying the loop style. For example, the following paper proposed many methods for semantic-preserving code transformations:

W. Zhang et al., Challenging Machine Learning-based Clone Detectors via Semantic-preserving Code Transformations, arXiv preprint arXiv:2111.10793,  Nov 2021.

Also, the idea proposed in the paper is not entirely novel, there has been a lot of work on generating adversarial examples for PLMs, including those on adversarial code generation:

Yang, Zhou, Jieke Shi, Junda He, and David Lo. "Natural Attack for Pre-trained Models of Code." arXiv preprint arXiv:2201.08698 (2022).

Jha, Akshita, and Chandan K. Reddy. "CodeAttack: Code-based Adversarial Attacks for Pre-Trained Programming Language Models." arXiv preprint arXiv: 2206.00052 (2022).

Unfortunately, this paper does not compare the proposed method with the related works.

The proposed method is only briefly described (only Section 3.3.2 involves the description of the proposed method). The description of the method lacks the corresponding theoretical description, which makes it difficult to understand the principles behind it. More descriptions are needed.

It would be better to use some downstream tasks to show the effectiveness of the adversarial samples generated by replacing variable names. Currently, there are no corresponding experiments to demonstrate the practical usefulness of the generated adversarial code.

The experimental metrics ASR and QT are not presented and the reasons for using them are not explained.

Minor:
Line 1 of Section 4: STOA → SOTA

content.title: Thanks for you review.
content.comment:
"Natural Attack for Pre-trained Models of Code" has been compared in our work. Variable-name replacement is one common method used by adversarial attack for code mode. The important thing is that how to do it better. Our approach is quite new and is very different from others, which we make full use of the real variable names and efficiently search the adversarial cases from real space instead of generation. 

Q1: Only considers variable name substitution？The proposed method considers only the variable name substitution. As the authors mentioned, there are other ways to keep the semantics unchanged such as modifying the loop style.

A1: The core idea of our algorithm is to efficiently search for replacement variables in the huge search space according to the changes of model behavior. For attacks such as modifying the loop style , they are rule based attacks. The search space is very limited, and we can directly use the traversal method to implement attacks. The advantages of our algorithm cannot be brought into play.

Q2: It would be better to use some downstream tasks to show the effectiveness of the adversarial samples generated by replacing variable names. Currently, there are no corresponding experiments to demonstrate the practical usefulness of the generated adversarial code.

A2: The generated confrontation samples can be used for confrontation training to improve the robustness of the model. How to use the confrontation samples and the original samples for efficient training is a subject we are studying.

Q3: The experimental metrics ASR and QT are not presented and the reasons for using them are not explained?
A3: In rebuttal revision, we have supplemented the definition of QT ,ASR and reasons for using them.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a black-box attack for generating (untargeted) adversarial examples on task-specific models fine-tuned from pre-trained models. The basic idea is to iterate over all variables in the program and identify substitute variable names. At each step, the best substitution that results in lowest probability for the ground truth label is identified and variables closest to it (within a delta) in the embedding space are selected for further exploration. The paper advocates that the variable names should be filtered by their length as well. An experimental evaluation on six classification tasks and three pre-trained models (total 18 models). The proposed approach under three variations is shown to outperform a baseline method MHM. Similar results are obtained for another baseline ALERT on 9 models and the attack is evaluated on adversarially-trained 3 models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

+ The problem of generating adversarial attacks on models of code is seeing active research.
+ The paper has evaluated the approach on several tasks and models, and comparison to baselines is performed.

**Weaknesses**
- Common constraints in black-box adversarial attacks are the number of queries that can be fired by the attacker (as each query has associated cost and possibility of detection) and what information is available (e.g., only top label). The paper does not provide means to address these, limiting its applicability. The paper considers untargeted adversarial attacks only.
- For fair evaluation, comparison with baselines should be done with the same query budget. The current setup does not appear to do that and how the "query times" is calculated is not described properly. The paper claims that the proposed attack has 11/18 lowest QT but that is over three variables of the proposed attack. The MHM attack is actually better or comparable compared to the individual variations, right? Further, why is ALERT evaluated only on 9/18 models?
- The paper needs careful rewrite. See the next section for detailed comments.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper needs careful rewrite to improve clarity. Some comments -
+ In the intro, should "additionally training a victim model" be "additionally training a substitute model"?
+ What is "semantic reservation"?
+ "data shit" -> "data shift"
+ Representaion at many places
+ attack access rate?
+ Section 3.3.2, what is change trending?
+ STOA?
+ Many others ...

The algorithm is not explained properly and has errors -
+ Are you considering all positions that a variable occurs in (Vars, Position)? Why are you referring to the first element as Vars if it is a single variable?
+ What do you mean by a group of pre-defined random variables?
+ Line 3 second assignment is syntactically incorrect.
+ Line 23 $var^{pre}$ can be undefined before use.

Validity of results -
+ The main metric "query times" is not defined. Is it time in seconds or the number of queries fired?
+ How do you compute the queries fired in an unsuccessful and a successful attack by different methods? 
+ How are the query times aggregated over a dataset? 
+ How do you select examples for attack for the attacks? 
+ What are the average number of queries by different attacks per example?
+ Why is ALERT evaluated only on 9/18 models?
+ The paper claims that the proposed attack has 11/18 lowest QT but that is over three variables of the proposed attack. The MHM attack is actually better or comparable compared to the individual variations, right?
+ What constraints are removed in the unlimited attack?
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes a potentially interesting solution but lacks significantly in clarity and validity of results.

content.title: Thanks for your review.
content.comment:
Black-box attacks have some constraints. For example, the server can detect the frequent querying IP address and block it. However, we can train a surrogate model.  

Q1: Common constraints in black-box adversarial attacks are the number of queries that can be fired by the attacker (as each query has associated cost and possibility of detection) and what information is available (e.g., only top label). The paper does not provide means to address these, limiting its applicability. The paper considers untargeted adversarial attacks only.

A1: Our algorithm limits the cost of the algorithm by limiting the number of iterations (6) and the number of candidate variables for each variable (60); We only used the top label of the victim model and its probability; Our paper only considers untargeted adversarial attacks and targeted adversarial attacks are the work we are studying.

Q2: For fair evaluation, comparison with baselines should be done with the same query budget. The current setup does not appear to do that and how the "query times" is calculated is not described properly. The paper claims that the proposed attack has 11/18 lowest QT but that is over three variables of the proposed attack. The MHM attack is actually better or comparable compared to the individual variations, right? Further, why is ALERT evaluated only on 9/18 models?

A2: In rebuttal revision, we have supplemented the definition of query time and the average query times required for each attack in each group of experiments,We use the average query time of each attack as the metric to evaluate the algorithm efficiency.We compared and evaluated the performance of Alert and MHM on 18 tasks，The experimental results show that RNNS outperforms MHM and ALERT in terms of ASR and QT. Specifically, RNNS achieves the best ASR and QT in 18 (out of 18) and 10 (out of 18) cases, respectively. If we compare each of RNNS version with MHM, we have 11/18 times lower QT, please read the table carefully.

Q3: What do you mean by a group of pre-defined random variables?
A3: We replace each variable with a group different-length names and measure the variance of the output to measure its uncertainty. This group of variables is composed of  predefined variables with different lengths.

- The attack is only based on variable renaming. It is not clear whether the technique can be extended to other forms of perturbation.

content.title: Thanks for your constructive advice.
content.comment:
Q1: The algorithm at a high level makes sense. However, the description is written poorly (3.3.2), almost impossible to understand the technical details.

A1: We have added a lot of content in the rebuttal revision to introduce the details of our algorithm. Please see 3.3.2

Q2: The attack is only based on variable renaming. It is not clear whether the technique can be extended to other forms of perturbation.

A2: The core idea of our algorithm is to efficiently search for replacement variables in the huge search space according to the changes of model behavior. For the code change/transformation such as modifying the loop style, they are rule based attacks. The search space is very limited, and we can directly use the traversal method to implement attacks. The advantages of our algorithm cannot be brought into play. 

Q3: Why for certain settings, RNNS-Direct is better than the other two is not clear. I would encourage the authors to give some intuitive explanations.

A3: This is closely related to the distribution of the variables in the task in the independent semantic space. If a large number of semantically similar variables are distributed near the seed variables in the current iteration, it is likely that after variable replacement, the probability of the ground truth label does not decreases, the algorithm ends, and the attack finally fails.
